catalog_quote: [Odden 2003, 2.3 Tone] All P-zone languages are tonal (though Ndengereko is losing distinctive prosody under Swahili influence). ... The most noteworthy feature of tone in zone P is the system of predictable verbal tones. Unlike most Bantu languages, there are no lexical contrasts in verb roots. Instead, surface tones are assigned to various positions, depending on tense-aspect. [Odden 2003, sec. 4, Ngindo forms] In Ngindo, the progressive is marked with -teenda- plus the infinitive (tl-teen-da ku-lím-a 'we were cultivating'). The past clitic -e of Matuumbi appears as -ge in Ndengereko (tl#lím-a-ge 'we were cultivating') and in Ngindo where it marks habituals (ba#lim-á-ge 'they cultivate'). ... new_statements.quote: Islam promotes the use of ki-Swahili, in which nearly all adult males and some women are bilingual along with kiNgindo, spoken for choice in the home. In addition the vernacular contains or has absorbed many Swahili features; but these are scarcely recognisable owing to the Ngindo practice of accentuating the first syllable of the stem, as opposed to the penultimate. Incidentally the Ngindo dialects follow Swahili in the hard pronunciation of the prefix 'ki-'.
new_statements.citation: Crosse-Upcott, A. R. W. 1956. The social structure of the KiNgindo-speaking peoples. PhD thesis, University of Cape Town.

Verbatim as reported; the text layer ( l. 2357) has only scanned noise ('Irt addition', 'penult.imate'). A a full-text search for stress/accent the whole 708-page text layer for accent|stress|tone|…
new_statements.rule_in_words: According to Crosse-Upcott (anthropologist, fieldwork in Ngindoland early 1950s), Ngindo places the word accent on the first syllable of the stem rather than on the penultimate syllable as Swahili does. This conflicts with Steere 1869 (preface to his Gindo/Zaramo/Ngazidja vocabularies: 'The accent invariably falls on the last syllable but one') and must be read against Odden 2003, the only specialist source, who classes Ngindo with all zone-P languages as tonal with tense-determined (non-lexical) verbal H tones, typically on the stem-initial vowel in the infinitive and many tenses (Ngindo ku-lím-a, cf. Matuumbi), and says nothing about stress. The stem-initial 'accent' heard by Crosse-Upcott is plausibly this grammatical stem-initial H; no modern description states a stress rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Crosse-Upcott. Odden's Ngindo data show the H elsewhere in some tenses (e.g. habitual ba#lim-á-ge with H on the final vowel of the stem), i.e. position is tense-dependent if the 'accent' is the grammatical H.
new_statements.domain_note: Crosse-Upcott's remark is an impressionistic word-level observation made to explain why Swahili loans sound different in Ngindo; not based on phonological analysis, no examples given. Steere's contrary penult statement is a one-line pronunciation note in a preface covering three languages. Odden 2003 (specialist, own field notes) treats Ngindo as a tone language.
new_statements.identity_note: Crosse-Upcott's remark concerns kiNgindo as spoken by the 'home-Ngindo' (Magingo and neighbouring sub-dialects) of the Liwale/Barikiwa area, i.e. Ngindo proper [ngin1244]; he treats Ndendeule [nden1249], Ndonde and Mbunga as 'Ngindo outlier' dialects but the accent sentence is about the home vernacular. Steere's 1869 'Gindo' vocabulary was collected from a Gindo speaker in Zanzibar and his accent sentence is a blanket preface note covering Gindo, Zaramo and Ngazidja together. Odden 2003's Ngindo data are his own Liwale-area field notes.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Ngindo has an empty rule; the one existing statement (Crosse-Upcott 1956, thesis p. 26) says Ngindo accentuates 'the first syllable of the stem, as opposed to the penultimate'. Steere's penultimate accent is exactly the placement Crosse-Upcott says Ngindo does NOT use. Caveat on weight: Steere's line is a one-sentence convention covering three languages, from Zanzibar informants, whereas Crosse-Upcott is Ngindo-specific and explicitly contrasts Ngindo with the Swahili penult. Odden 2003 (held by the project, already consulted) treats Ngindo as tonal and says nothing about stress. babel.hathitrust.org (pt, view=plaintext, imgsrv plaintext, pt/search) returned not reach…
new_statements.rule_in_words: A blanket pronunciation note for the whole pamphlet (Gindo, Zaramo and Angazidja/Comorian vocabularies): Italian vowels, English consonants, and the accent always on the penultimate syllable. It is a spelling/reading convention stated once for all three languages, not a Gindo-specific observation.
new_statements.identity_note: Steere's 'Gindo' (Kigindo) was recorded in Zanzibar from freed slave boys (seq-11 token bag: Gindos, Yaos, Nyassas, Kilwa, Lake Nyassa, Zanzibar, school, slave, boys, informant names Hamisi, Gilbert, Harry, John) described as a tribe lying between Kilwa on the coast and Lake Nyassa, i.e. the Ngindo of the Kilwa/Liwale hinterland; Glottolog files the work under ngin1244. The accent sentence itself is not Gindo-specific: it closes the signed Advertisement and applies to all three vocabularies (Gindo, Zaramo, Angazidja = Ngazidja Comorian).

readall_conflicts: Steere 1869 (blanket note for the pamphlet's three vocabularies, Gindo included): 'The accent invariably falls on the last syllable but one' = fixed penultimate. Crosse-Upcott 1956 (Ngindo-specific, thesis p. 26, verified against the page image earlier): Swahili loans are 'scarcely recognisable owing to the Ngindo practice of accentuating the first syllable of the stem, as opposed to the penultimate' = stem-initial, explicitly not penultimate. Odden 2003 (Nurse & Philippson, p. 534): all P-zone languages are tonal, Ngindo verb forms tone-marked, no stress statement. The two accent statements disagree on placement (penult vs stem-initial); Steere's is a one-line reading convention over three languages collected from Zanzibar informants in 1869 and carries little weight against Crosse-Upcott's language-specific contrast, but neither is a phonological analysis, and the language is reported as tonal.
